prompt: Each 100 MB download selects 10 MB/s or 90 MB/s with equal probability and keeps that speed throughout. Ignoring overhead, what is its expected duration?

options.explanation: Correct. Half the time it takes 100/10 = 10 s and half the time 100/90 ≈ 1.1 s, so the mean duration is 5 + 0.556 ≈ 5.56 s.

100 / 50 uses the average speed, i.e. assumes the mean duration equals 100 divided by the expected speed. That equality fails for this nonconstant two-speed distribution; nonlinearity alone would not rule out equality in every distribution.
10 s is the time at the slow speed only. Half the time the download is much faster.
That is the time at the fast speed only.

workedExample:
The time is a non-linear function of the speed, so average the times, not the speeds.

```formula
T = D / S
E[T] = 0.5 × (100 MB / (10 MB/s))
  + 0.5 × (100 MB / (90 MB/s))
E[T] = 0.5 × 10 s + 0.5 × (10/9) s
E[T] ≈ (5 + 0.556) s ≈ 5.56 s
D / E[S] = 100 MB / (50 MB/s)
D / E[S] = 2 s
where
T: the download duration, in seconds (s)
D: the fixed download size, 100 megabytes (MB)
S: the speed chosen for an entire transfer, either 10 or 90 megabytes per second (MB/s), each with probability 0.5
E[ ]: expected value, in the units of the quantity averaged
MB: megabyte, one million bytes
s: second, the time unit
≈: approximately equal to, from rounding
Expectations: all displayed expectations are finite; an expectation has the units of the quantity averaged
In words: half the downloads take ten seconds and half take ten-ninths of a second, giving about 5.56 seconds on average; dividing by the mean speed incorrectly predicts two seconds.
```

Because 1/S is **convex** (it curves upwards), **Jensen's inequality** says the expected value of 1/S is at least 1 divided by the expected speed: the slower transfers contribute more to expected duration.
